from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Nature of Light Waves", [
            "Light travels as a constant wave in a vacuum.",
            "Optical density measures how a medium slows light down.",
            "Denser materials cause light to slow down significantly."
        ])
        
        # Define base elements
        wave = FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(4 * x), x_range=[-PI, PI], color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(wave, 'B2', 'D5')
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(wave), run_time=2)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.play(Create(wavelength_arrow))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        self.play(Create(amplitude_arrow))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(RED))
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application: The Archer Fish", [
            "Archer fish navigate refraction to catch prey.",
            "Light bends at the water's surface.",
            "The fish compensates for the apparent position."
        ])
        
        water_surface = Line(self.grid["C1"], self.grid["C6"], color=BLUE)
        water = Rectangle(width=5.0, height=3.0, fill_color=BLUE, fill_opacity=0.3, stroke_width=0)
        water.next_to(water_surface, DOWN, buff=0)
        
        fish = Circle(radius=0.2, color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=1).move_to(self.grid["E3"])
        prey = Dot(self.grid["A4"], color=RED, radius=0.1)
        
        ray_to_surface = Line(prey.get_center(), self.grid["C4"], color=WHITE)
        ray_to_fish = Line(self.grid["C4"], fish.get_center(), color=WHITE)
        
        apparent_prey = Dot(self.grid["B5"], color=RED, radius=0.08).set_opacity(0.5)
        virtual_ray = DashedLine(apparent_prey.get_center(), self.grid["C4"], color=YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.add(water, water_surface, fish, prey)
        self.play(FadeIn(fish), FadeIn(prey))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.play(Create(ray_to_surface), Create(ray_to_fish))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(RED))
        self.play(FadeIn(apparent_prey), Create(virtual_ray))
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary and Conclusion", [
            "Light changes direction when speed changes.",
            "Refraction depends on the refractive index.",
            "The normal line is our reference point."
        ])
        
        # Animation Elements
        light_ray = Line(start=ORIGIN, end=RIGHT*2, color=YELLOW)
        normal_line = DashedLine(start=UP*2, end=DOWN*2, color=WHITE)
        quiz_text = Text("If light enters a medium\nwith a higher n, does it bend\ntoward or away from normal?", font_size=24, color=BLUE)
        answer_text = Text("Answer: Toward", font_size=32, color=GREEN)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(light_ray, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(light_ray))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        self.place_at_grid(quiz_text, 'D3', scale_factor=0.7)
        self.play(FadeIn(quiz_text))
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(normal_line, 'C4', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(normal_line))
        self.place_at_grid(answer_text, 'E4', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Write(answer_text))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Physics of Refraction: Why Light Bends

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Nature of Light Waves
sections.content: Briefly define light as an electromagnetic wave traveling at a constant speed (c) in a vacuum. Introduce the concept of 'Optical Density'—how much a medium slows down light. Visual: A light wave pulse moving through a vacuum vs. a dense medium.
sections.example: Imagine light as a car moving from a smooth highway (vacuum) onto a muddy field (glass); the tires on one side hit the mud first, causing the car to pivot.

sections.title: Defining Refraction and Snell's Law
sections.content: Explain refraction as the change in direction of a wave passing from one medium to another. Introduce Snell's Law (n1sinθ1 = n2sinθ2) using an animated diagram showing the angle of incidence vs. angle of refraction relative to the 'normal' line.
sections.example: Show a laser pointer hitting a glass block at an angle, highlighting the normal line and the bending toward the normal as it enters the denser material.

sections.title: The Refractive Index (n)
sections.content: Explain the formula n = c / v. Use a bar chart visualization to compare the refractive indices of air (1.0), water (1.33), and diamond (2.42) to emphasize how higher 'n' equals slower speed and sharper bending.
sections.example: A 'Speedometer Animation' showing light pulses moving faster in air than in diamond, visualizing why diamond is more 'optically dense'.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Archer Fish
sections.content: Apply the concept to a biological context. The archer fish must compensate for refraction when spitting at prey above the water. Explain that the fish perceives the insect's 'apparent position' higher than its 'actual position'.
sections.example: Visual overlay of an archer fish looking up: The light from the beetle bends at the water surface, so the fish aims slightly below the apparent image to hit the actual target.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap: Light changes speed when hitting different media, causing a change in direction (refraction). Remind students that the 'Normal' line is the universal reference point for all refraction calculations.
sections.example: A quick-fire quiz screen: 'If light enters a medium with a higher refractive index, does it bend toward or away from the normal?' (Answer: Toward).
